organism: Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcus), a lancet-shaped, gram-positive, facultative anaerobic bacterium, usually seen as diplococci. Most strains are encapsulated; the capsular polysaccharide is both the main virulence factor and the basis for serotyping - 100 serotypes were documented as of 2020. Most serotypes can cause serious disease, but only a handful account for most actual infections, and which ones dominate varies by age group and geography.
clinicalFeaturesSummary: The major invasive syndromes are pneumonia, bacteremia, and meningitis. In adults, pneumococcal pneumonia (the most common presentation) has a short incubation of 1-3 days and presents with abrupt fever, chills, pleuritic chest pain, and productive cough; case-fatality for pneumonia with bacteremia is around 10%. Bacteremia without pneumonia (over 5,000 US cases/year) carries about 12% case-fatality; meningitis has roughly 14% case-fatality in adults with common neurologic sequelae among survivors. In children under 2, bacteremia without a known infection site is the most common invasive presentation (about 40% of invasive disease in this age group), followed by bacteremic pneumonia (25%-30%); pneumococcus has become the leading cause of bacterial meningitis in children under 5 since Hib's decline. Pneumococci are also a very common cause of acute otitis media - detected in 24%-31% of middle ear aspirates, with more than 60% of children having had at least one episode by 12 months.
epidemiologySummary: Humans are the only reservoir - the organism lives in the nasopharynx of asymptomatic carriers (5%-90% of healthy people depending on age and setting; 20%-60% of school-age children versus only 5%-10% of adults without children, though up to 50%-60% on some military installations). Transmission is via respiratory droplets or autoinoculation from one's own carried bacteria. Infections are more common in winter and early spring. The period of communicability is unknown but presumed to last as long as the organism is present in respiratory secretions.
secularTrendsSummary: An estimated 31,000+ cases and 3,500+ deaths from invasive pneumococcal disease occurred in the US in 2017, more than half in adults with a vaccine indication. Before routine conjugate vaccination (introduced 2000), children under 5 bore an estimated 17,000 invasive cases and 200 deaths annually, plus about 5 million cases of acute otitis media. PCV7 (2000) drove a 99% decline in invasive disease caused by its 7 covered serotypes in children, partly offset by a rise in non-vaccine serotypes (especially 19A); PCV13 (2010), which added 19A and 5 other serotypes, drove a further 90% decline in PCV13-serotype disease in children, with reductions sustained and not offset by new serotype replacement. Adults have benefited indirectly too - PCV13-serotype disease fell more than 60% among adults 65+ through herd effects of childhood vaccination. Coverage gaps remain: only 24.5% of adults 19-64 at increased risk had been vaccinated as of 2017, and more than 65% of people hospitalized with severe pneumococcal disease had a prior hospitalization in the preceding 3-5 years without having received the vaccine.
vaccineDescription: Two vaccine types are used in the US: PPSV23 (Pneumovax 23, licensed 1983, replacing an earlier 14-valent vaccine), a 23-serotype purified polysaccharide vaccine given IM or subcutaneously with phenol preservative, no adjuvant; and PCV13 (Prevnar 13, licensed 2010, replacing 7-valent PCV7 from 2000), a 13-serotype polysaccharide-protein conjugate (CRM197, a nontoxic diphtheria toxin variant) given IM with aluminum phosphate adjuvant, no antibiotic or preservative. The two vaccines work differently - conjugation makes PCV13 immunogenic in infants and produces a durable T-cell-dependent response, while polysaccharide-only PPSV23 elicits a T-cell-independent response that doesn't reliably 'boost' on revaccination.
vaccinationScheduleSummary: All children 2-59 months should routinely receive PCV13 (3-dose primary series at 2, 4, 6 months plus a 12-15 month booster; minimum interval 4 weeks before age 1, 8 weeks at 1+); unvaccinated children starting later need fewer doses depending on age at the first dose. All adults 65+ should receive a single dose of PPSV23. People 2 and older with specific chronic or immunocompromising conditions may need PCV13, PPSV23, or both, with exact timing depending on the condition and prior vaccination history (see Risk-Based Vaccination). PCV13 and PPSV23 should never be given on the same clinic day - when both are indicated, PCV13 should come first, followed by PPSV23 at least 8 weeks later for adults with immunocompromising conditions or 1 year later for immunocompetent adults (giving them simultaneously or too close together does not require repeating either dose in adults, but does require repeating PCV13 in children).
vaccineEfficacySummary: PPSV23: more than 80% of healthy adults develop antibody to covered serotypes within 2-3 weeks, persisting at least 5 years in healthy adults but declining faster in those with chronic illness or immunodeficiency; overall clinical effectiveness against invasive disease from covered serotypes is 60%-70%. Antibody response in children under 2 is generally poor, and revaccination doesn't reliably boost titers given the T-cell-independent immune response. There's no consensus PPSV23 prevents non-bacteremic pneumonia, so providers should avoid calling it simply a 'pneumonia vaccine.' PCV13: the earlier PCV7 reduced invasive disease from its covered serotypes by 97% in a landmark trial; PCV13 was licensed based on comparable immunogenicity to PCV7, and a large Dutch placebo-controlled trial in adults 65+ later found 45.6% efficacy against vaccine-type pneumococcal pneumonia and 75.0% efficacy against vaccine-type invasive disease.
contraindicationsSummary: A severe allergic reaction to a vaccine component or a prior dose is a contraindication for both PCV13 and PPSV23. Moderate or severe acute illness is a precaution. ACIP has no specific recommendation on PCV13 use during pregnancy; PPSV23 safety in pregnancy hasn't been formally studied, though no adverse outcomes have been reported after inadvertent vaccination - women at increased risk who are vaccine candidates should ideally be vaccinated before becoming pregnant.
vaccineSafetySummary: PPSV23: local reactions (pain, soreness, swelling, induration), headache, fatigue, and muscle pain are most common, usually resolving within 48 hours; adults 65+ tend to have more systemic reactions after a second dose than a first. A transient increase in viral replication has been reported in HIV-positive people after PPSV23, without associated clinical or immunologic deterioration. PCV13: local reactions plus decreased appetite, fatigue, headache, muscle pain, irritability, and fever (plus altered sleep in infants/toddlers) are most common. Simultaneous PCV13 and inactivated influenza vaccine in young children has been associated with an increased febrile-seizure risk in some influenza seasons - the seizures are brief with no long-term complications, and this has not changed vaccination recommendations. Postlicensure VAERS review for both vaccines has been consistent with prelicensure findings.
vaccineStorageSummary: PCV13 and PPSV23 must be stored at refrigerator temperature, 2C to 8C (36F to 46F). See CDC's Vaccine Storage and Handling Toolkit for complete guidance.
surveillanceSummary: Invasive pneumococcal disease is notifiable in most states. Definitive diagnosis relies on culturing the organism from blood or another normally sterile site; a urinary antigen test is also available for adult community-acquired pneumonia and can detect infection even after antibiotics have started. See CDC's Manual for the Surveillance of Vaccine-Preventable Diseases for reporting guidance.

supplementalTopics.title: Risk-Based Vaccination for Children and Adolescents
supplementalTopics.summary: Beyond routine PCV13 in early childhood, children 2 years and older with certain conditions need additional doses. A CSF leak or cochlear implant warrants PCV13 (if not already complete) plus PPSV23 at least 8 weeks later, at any age. Functional/anatomic asplenia (including sickle cell disease) or an immunocompromising condition (congenital/acquired immunodeficiency, malignancy on immunosuppressive therapy, HIV, chronic renal failure, nephrotic syndrome, organ transplant, or immunosuppressive medication) warrants the same PCV13-then-PPSV23 sequence PLUS a second PPSV23 dose 5 years after the first. Chronic heart/lung disease, diabetes, chronic liver disease, or (in adults) smoking or alcoholism only trigger a PPSV23 recommendation, not PCV13, in the 2-18 age range specifically (unlike the same conditions in adults 19-64, where a single PPSV23 dose still applies) - PCV13 is not indicated for these conditions once a child is out of the routine vaccination age window.

supplementalTopics.title: Risk-Based Vaccination for Adults 19-64
supplementalTopics.summary: Routine PCV13/PPSV23 vaccination is not recommended for healthy adults 19-64. Unvaccinated adults in this age range with chronic heart/lung disease, diabetes, chronic liver disease, smoking, or alcoholism should get a single PPSV23 dose only. Unvaccinated adults with an immunocompromising condition, CSF leak, or cochlear implant should get PCV13 followed by PPSV23 at least 8 weeks later (or PCV13 at least 1 year after PPSV23 if PPSV23 came first); those with asplenia or an immunocompromising condition additionally need a second PPSV23 dose 5 years after the first.

supplementalTopics.title: Vaccination of Adults 65 and Older
supplementalTopics.summary: Every adult 65 or older should get a single lifetime dose of PPSV23, regardless of prior pneumococcal vaccination history (a dose given before 65 doesn't count - a final dose is needed at 65 or at least 5 years after the last PPSV23 dose, whichever is later; a dose already given at 65+ doesn't need to be repeated). Adults 65+ without an immunocompromising condition, CSF leak, or cochlear implant may decide with their clinician whether to also receive PCV13 (shared clinical decision-making) - if so, PCV13 should come first, followed by PPSV23 at least 1 year later. Notably, self-reported PPSV23 history (but not PCV13 history) is acceptable evidence of vaccination for adults, unlike the written documentation normally required for other vaccines.

supplementalTopics.title: Timing Around Elective Procedures
supplementalTopics.summary: When a splenectomy, immunocompromising therapy, or cochlear implant placement is being planned, vaccines should ideally be completed before the procedure - PCV13 first, then PPSV23 at least 8 weeks later, with PPSV23 given at least 2 weeks before the treatment or surgery itself if there isn't time for the full 8-week gap. If treatment or surgery can't be delayed, vaccination can be given afterward instead. A person scheduled for splenectomy should be treated as already asplenic for purposes of applying these recommendations.

keyPoints: S. pneumoniae was first isolated by Louis Pasteur in 1881, but wasn't reliably distinguished from other pneumonias until the Gram stain (1884)
PCV13 and PPSV23 must never be given on the same clinic visit - when both are needed, PCV13 comes first

PCV7 introduction in children drove a 99% decline in disease from its covered serotypes, but was partly offset by a rise in non-covered serotypes (especially 19A) - which PCV13 was specifically designed to address
Childhood conjugate vaccination has produced substantial indirect (herd) protection in adults 65+ through reduced transmission
More than 65% of people hospitalized with severe pneumococcal disease had a hospitalization in the prior 3-5 years without having been vaccinated - a recognized missed-opportunity gap
Self-reported PPSV23 vaccination history is acceptable evidence, unlike the written documentation required for most other vaccines including PCV13
Providers should avoid calling PPSV23 a 'pneumonia vaccine' - there's no consensus it prevents non-bacteremic pneumococcal pneumonia specifically
